stem: A facility permits a routine laboratory specimen to be sent through its validated pneumatic tube system. What should the nurse do before sending it?

options.A: Confirm the specimen is correctly identified, securely closed, and placed in the facility-approved leak-resistant transport packaging for the pneumatic system.
options.B: Loosen the specimen cap so pressure changes during transport can escape through the container opening.
options.C: Remove patient identification because the pneumatic carrier itself provides sufficient specimen identity.
options.D: Place an unsealed specimen directly into the pneumatic carrier because the transport system prevents leakage by design.

rationale: CDC laboratory-safety guidance states that pneumatic-tube use should be governed by facility procedures and risk assessment because specimen breakage or leakage can contaminate the system. Specimens should be in intact, secure containers, and leakproof primary/secondary containment is a core transport principle. A is therefore appropriate for a routine specimen in a validated system. B and D deliberately increase leakage risk, and C creates an identification error.
educational_objective: Before pneumatic-tube transport of an approved routine specimen, verify correct identification, secure closure, and facility-approved leak-resistant containment.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Guidelines for Safe Work Practices in Human and Animal Medical Diagnostic Laboratories
source_version_date: MMWR Supplement 2012; currentness rechecked against current CDC pneumatic-tube risk-assessment guidance on 2026-08-16
source_locator: Section 3.1 Specimen Receiving and Log-In/Setup Station; 3.1.6 Pneumatic tube systems; 4.1.3 Leaking containers
source_claim_supported: Pneumatic-tube specimen transport requires SOP/risk assessment; unsealed containers can be inappropriate; leakage can contaminate the transport system; specimens should use leakproof containment.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Printed p.8, Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Follow procedures for handling biohazardous materials; Properly identify client when providing care; Facilitate appropriate and safe use of equipment
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — safe specimen transport

source_original.stem: A facility permits a routine laboratory specimen to be sent through its validated pneumatic tube system. What should the nurse do before sending it?

options.A: Seal and label the specimen correctly and use the facility-approved leak-resistant transport packaging
options.B: Loosen the container cap so pressure changes during transit can escape through the specimen opening
options.C: Remove patient identification because the pneumatic carrier itself provides adequate specimen identity
options.D: Place an unsealed specimen directly in the carrier because tube systems prevent leakage by design

source_original.rationale: Specimens must be properly identified and transported in secure, leak-resistant containers according to laboratory and facility policy. Pneumatic systems require validation for the specimen type; some high-risk specimens should not be sent by pneumatic tube.
source_original.source_detail: Specimen transport: leakproof primary container and sealable leakproof transport packaging; MMWR Suppl. 2012; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Retained the validated-system scenario, clarified correct identification plus secure closure and approved leak-resistant containment, and documented current CDC risk-assessment guidance without universalizing pneumatic-tube use to high-risk specimens.

audit_findings.source_authority: CDC laboratory safety guidance; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: Core CDC safe-work-practice document is older, but current CDC specimen guidance continues to require pneumatic-tube risk assessment and safe specimen containment.
audit_findings.claim_audit: CDC directly supports pneumatic-system SOP/risk assessment, intact/secure containers, and leakproof transport containment.

distractor_audit.A: Correct and consistent with safe containment/identification.
distractor_audit.B: Loosening the cap creates leakage risk.
distractor_audit.C: Removing identification is unsafe and contradicts client/specimen identification requirements.
distractor_audit.D: PTS breakage/leakage is a documented contamination risk; unsealed transport is inappropriate.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A preserves identity and containment within the stem's already-validated-system condition.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices concern preparation immediately before pneumatic transport; no alternate safe approach is offered.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN p.8 covers biohazard handling, client identification, and safe equipment use.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked CDC PTS sections and current risk-assessment guidance, challenged whether the item could imply universal pneumatic-tube safety, and confirmed the 'facility permits/validated routine specimen' qualifier resolves that issue. A remained uniquely correct.
